title: Bag of Tricks for Image Classification with Convolutional Neural Networks
authors: Tong He, Zhi Zhang, Hang Zhang, Zhongyue Zhang, Junyuan Xie, Mu Li

pages.title: The unsung refinements behind accuracy gains
pages.subtitle: Why the training recipe matters as much as the architecture

blocks.html: Much of the progress in image classification is credited to new architectures, but a surprising share of it comes from quiet refinements in how networks are trained — data augmentation tweaks, learning-rate schedules, small architecture adjustments. These 'tricks' are often buried in implementation details or mentioned only in passing, yet stacked together they make a large difference.

This paper does the unglamorous but valuable work of cataloguing these refinements, ablating each one, and reporting the cumulative gain on ImageNet. The result: a vanilla ResNet-50 is pushed from 75.3% to 79.29% top-1 accuracy — better than many newer architectures — just by improving the training procedure.

By combining these refinements together, we raise ResNet-50's top-1 validation accuracy from 75.3% to 79.29% on ImageNet, and show that improvements transfer to object detection and semantic segmentation.

The tricks fall into three groups: efficient training (large-batch and low-precision tricks), model tweaks (small surgical changes to the ResNet architecture), and training refinements (schedule and regularization tricks).

pages.title: Large-batch training: warmup and the linear scaling rule
pages.subtitle: Training fast without losing accuracy

blocks.html: Larger mini-batches make better use of GPUs but tend to hurt accuracy if the learning rate is left unchanged. Two tricks fix this.
Linear scaling rule. A larger batch gives a less noisy gradient estimate, so you can afford a proportionally larger step. Scale the learning rate linearly with batch size:
Read this as: start from the standard learning rate 0.1 for batch size 256, and scale it up in proportion to the batch size b.

Learning-rate warmup. At the very start, the weights are random and a large learning rate can destabilize training. So begin with a small rate and ramp it linearly up to the target over the first few epochs, letting the network settle before taking big steps.

items: Zero gamma initialization: set the last BatchNorm $\gamma$ in each residual block to 0, so each block starts as an identity and the network is easier to train early on.
No bias decay: apply weight decay only to convolution and fully-connected weights, not to biases or to BatchNorm's $\gamma$ and $\beta$, to avoid over-regularizing those parameters.

blocks.html: Modern GPUs are much faster in 16-bit floating point (FP16) than in 32-bit (FP32). Training in FP16 — while keeping an FP32 master copy of the weights for stable accumulation — speeds up training substantially and, somewhat surprisingly, can even slightly improve accuracy.

Combined with the large-batch tricks above, switching to a batch size of 1024 in FP16 trained ResNet-50 faster and reached marginally higher accuracy than the FP32 baseline, showing these efficiency tricks are not a speed-versus-accuracy tradeoff.

pages.title: ResNet-B, -C, and -D
pages.subtitle: Three small surgical changes to the downsampling path

blocks.html: These are tiny modifications to the ResNet architecture that barely change the parameter count but recover information the original design throws away, mostly around the downsampling blocks.

items: ResNet-B: in the downsampling residual path, the original 1x1 convolution with stride 2 skips three-quarters of the input pixels. ResNet-B moves the stride to the following 3x3 convolution so no information is ignored.
ResNet-C: replace the expensive 7x7 stem convolution with three stacked 3x3 convolutions, which is cheaper and slightly more accurate.

ResNet-D: in the shortcut (skip) path of the downsampling block, the 1x1 stride-2 convolution also drops pixels; ResNet-D adds a 2x2 average-pooling step before it so the shortcut keeps all the information.

blocks.html: Each tweak adds negligible computation but contributes a fraction of a percent, and together (ResNet-D) they account for about a 1% top-1 improvement — a good deal for changes that leave the model essentially the same size.

pages.title: Cosine learning-rate decay
pages.subtitle: A smoother schedule than step decay

blocks.html: Instead of dropping the learning rate by a factor of 10 at fixed milestones (step decay), cosine decay lowers it smoothly following a half-cosine curve from the initial value down to zero over training:

Read this as: at step t of T total steps, scale the base rate by a cosine that starts at 1 and eases down to 0. The high rate early explores, and the gentle decay late lets the model converge precisely without the abrupt jolts of step decay.

pages.title: Label smoothing, mixup, and knowledge distillation
pages.subtitle: Regularizing the targets and the training data

blocks.html: Label smoothing. Hard one-hot labels push the network to be over-confident, which hurts generalization. Label smoothing replaces the target 1 with $1 - \varepsilon$ and spreads the remaining $\varepsilon$ mass over the other classes, so the model aims for a slightly softened distribution and calibrates better.

Mixup. Train on convex combinations of pairs of examples and their labels: a new sample is $\lambda x_i + (1-\lambda) x_j$ with label $\lambda y_i + (1-\lambda) y_j$. This strong data augmentation smooths the decision boundary and improves robustness, though it benefits from training longer.

Knowledge distillation. Use a more accurate teacher network (e.g., ResNet-152) to provide soft targets that a student (ResNet-50) tries to match in addition to the true labels, transferring some of the teacher's knowledge.
The heart of the paper is the progression: start from a baseline ResNet-50 and add the refinements one at a time, watching top-1 ImageNet accuracy climb. The approximate cumulative trajectory:

rows: + Efficient training (large batch, FP16, warmup, zero-gamma, no-bias-decay)

blocks.html: No single trick is dramatic on its own, but they accumulate to a roughly 4-point top-1 gain — turning a stock ResNet-50 into a model competitive with much newer architectures, all without changing the fundamental network.

pages.title: Transfer and takeaways
pages.subtitle: The gains are not just ImageNet trivia

blocks.html: A natural worry is that these tricks merely overfit the ImageNet classification benchmark. The authors show the opposite: the improved backbones transfer to downstream tasks, giving better results on object detection and semantic segmentation, evidence that the refinements produce genuinely better features rather than benchmark-specific gains.

items: Training procedure matters as much as architecture; small, well-known tricks compound into large gains.
Efficient training: linear LR scaling, warmup, zero-gamma init, no-bias-decay, and FP16 low-precision.
Model tweaks: ResNet-B/C/D fix information loss in the stem and downsampling blocks for ~1% at almost no cost.
Training refinements: cosine LR decay, label smoothing, mixup, and knowledge distillation.
Cumulatively, ResNet-50 goes from 75.3% to 79.29% top-1 on ImageNet, and the gains transfer to detection and segmentation.
